newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa may need to import gasoline in 1996 - BP.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa may need to import gasoline in 1996 - BP.

text.p: Sharply rising demand means South Africa could run out of gasoline refining capacity as early as this year, forcing imports of the product, BP Africa managing director John Greensmith said on Monday.

"Petrol is effectively starting to run out this year...we do see, because of the very rapid growth, the start of importation this year even and certainly next year," he told AIC Africa Oil Conference here.
Greensmith said he could not predict how much would have to be imported this year or next, but told Reuters that scheduled shutdowns pointed to an extremely tight position by the year-end.
South Africa currently has three oil refineries at Cape Town, Durban and in the interior processing 400,00 to 450,000 barrels a day.

The country's oil industry has long debated the need for additional capacity, but oil companies have been reluctant to commit themselves pending clarfication of plans to liberalise the domestic oil market.
Greensmith said BP figures showed South African oil consumption grew by 8.7 percent last year, far outstripping overall growth in gross domestic product of 3.3 percent.

A similar picture of accelerating growth for oil -- albeit of a low base -- was being experienced elsewhere in sub-Saharan Africa, he said. Africa currently accounted for a meagre three percent of global petroleum consumption, but this was increasing sharply in several southern and eastern African countries.

Uganda, for example, had seen demand increase by between 10 and 12 percent last year and other countries had seen demand up by over five percent after years of negative growth, as car usage increases.
Outside South Africa the region has three significant refineries in Tanzania, Kenya and Zambia.
Of these Greensmith said Kenya might have the potential to be expanded and developed as a regional supply centre located half-way between South Africa and the Gulf.
African countries had to get away from the idea of oil refineries as prestige enterprises similar to a national airline and instead focus on the economics of processing oil, Greensmith said.
In the past the World Bank has voiced concern about the inefficiency of regional African oil refineries.
